children.comment:
Slide
This move has been around for ages but is no longer the most common one. Some professionals (such as [Yeonwoo Cho in 2019](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUetCMEW4Cc&t=53) and [Michael Redmond in 2020](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MzglC0kVQTY&t=142s)) have noted a decrease in the AI winning percentage once played and called it slightly bad. True enough, this slide has little effect on Black, who needn't respond locally. But modern AI doesn't entirely shun it. In fact, it's occasionally the preferred move of modern AI such as Tencent's FineArt. It can be recommended when taking sente isn't so important and for double-digit kyu players because it's simple. Otherwise, attaching may be preferred, as in .

It is named after Kobayashi Koichi who used it steadily at one point in his career. This fuseki has been actively played for some 20 years now. It is an aggressive, fighting strategy.

Two-Space Extension

The primary objective of this extension is to ensure Black's own safety rather than to attack White. If White is thick at the lower side, this extension also forestalls an attack while erasing that thickness.

This is undeniably a negative attitude. Still, it is part of the professional repertoire, and AI evaluates it similarly to the more common move Q14. This extension is submissive by comparison but has the added benefit of not being vulnerable to approach at R12.

children.comment:
Two-Space Low Pincer
Popular in the 17th century, this pincer is still played in contemporary games. Contrary to its former "leisurely" reputation (according to Hideo Otake and others), this move can spark fighting after White Q15 (see ). AI analysis scores the fight as relatively equal, diverging from traditional expectations. If White opts out of the fight, the game might continue with simple moves.
